utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Russo, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that you are calling ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution calls Murray Douglas Dawes, Witness 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dawes. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Dawes, you will first be examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution, and you will find him to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Murray Douglas Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, do you recall giving two statements to the ICTY, the first dated 21 and 22 August of 1996; and the second dated the 2nd of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5502.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, do you recognise this as your statement you made 21 and 22 August of 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Presiding Judge's microphone be turned off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now please have 65 ter 5503.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at the screen, Mr. Dawes, do you recognise this as the statement you gave dated 2 April 2008?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dawes, did you have a chance to review both of those statements prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in that review, can you say whether those statements accurately reflect what you said to the investigators at the time?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the course of reviewing those statements, did you note a few corrections and clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could, I'd like to take you briefly through those, the first being, I believe, you indicated that references in your statements to WO or Warrant Officer Engleby are incorrect, and that Sergeant Engleby was, by rank, a Sergeant at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And we don't need to move to these, I don't believe; but on page 7 of your first statement, Mr. Dawes, it indicates that General Forand authorised the dispensation of fuel to civilians who came to the gate of the UN compound on the evening of 4 August, and you assumed that approximately 3.000 litres of fuel was given out to these civilians. And I believe you indicated you wanted to clarify the fact that you were not certain of the amount of 3.000 litres and that you could not recall where that figure came from. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I believe you also wanted to add, with regard to the dispensation of fuel, that General Leslie had told you also at that time that fuel either had been given out or would be given out to ARSK soldiers in order allow them to leave the area of Sector South. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again on page 7, you stated: "The shelling commenced at approximately 0500 hours in the morning of the 5th August. Again, it was heavy and direct fire as well." I believe you indicated that you wanted to clarify that your reference to "direct fire" meant tank fire that you could hear outside of the town of Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, on page 7, in that same portion, you indicate that: "Approximately 50 mainly old people from the front line areas had gathered in front of the main gate." And I believe you wanted to clarify that these were civilians who lived in the villages near the front line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, finally, on page 11 of your first statement, you discuss finding the body of a man named Milan Babic in a hamlet in the area of Prijici. I believe you wanted to clarify that you were told by the two women who showed you where this body was that Milan Babic was a Croat, and that the hamlet in which he was found was a Croat hamlet which had been under the protection of the UN prior to Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, may I take to you page 4, line 3, I did not hear you. Could you please repeat what you said there. I believe you also wanted to add that "with regard to the," and then it reads "disp" on the transcript. I missed that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That was intended to read "with regard to the dispensation of fuel that had been given out ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, taking into account the corrections and clarifications we've just reviewed, is the information provided in both of your statements, all taken together, true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were examined with regard to those same matters here in Court today, would your answers be the same as in those statements?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would move for the admission of 65 ters 5502 and 5503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the written submissions, I understand that there is no objection against admission. Mr. Registrar, the August 1996 statement would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P980, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P980 is admitted into evidence. The April 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P981 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could please have the assistance of the court usher, I'd like to hand hard copies of the statements to Mr. Dawes. With the Court's permission, I would like to read a relatively brief 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Murray Douglas Dawes was an UN accommodation officer employed by the Canadian agency Care Canada and was based there Knin from May of 1994 to October 1995. In the days immediately prior to Operation Storm, he observed that the majority of inhabitants in Knin were women, children, and the elderly since most of the men were at the front lines. He visited the main ARSK barracks in Knin on several occasions prior to Operation Storm, including on 3 August 1995, and observed that there were not many soldiers and no heavy weapons in the town. Mr. Dawes was present in Knin during the artillery attack and made several trips into Knin on 4 August to rescue UN and local civilian employees. He observed and felt the effects of the artillery and rockets which were fired into the town, including observing dead civilians and shelling damage in the residential and farming areas in Knin. On the afternoon of 4 August, Mr. Dawes was slightly injured by a shell which impacted approximately ten metres from the ECMM headquarters, which was located in the area near the hospital. He observed some ARSK soldiers in Knin on 4 August, some of whom had attempted to hijack his APC and others who had abandoned Strmica to assist in the withdrawal of troops from the front line. On 6 August, Mr. Dawes travelled into Knin and witnessed HV soldiers and civilian policemen openly looting the town. There were individuals in orange coveralls cleaning the streets and pavements and other individuals in hazmat-type outfits removing dead bodies and spoiled food from the houses. Also on 6 August, he travelled to Vrbnik and Kistanje where he witnessed HV soldiers looting and destroying houses from the inside. Along the road he travelled on 6 August, he saw many dead civilians who he believes were killed by small-arms fire because of the bullet holes in and around their vehicles. On 8 August, he travelled along the Knin-Drnis road where he witnessed HV soldiers and civilians looting, as well as what he described as well-disciplined Croatian troops in black uniforms burning houses. Mr. President, that concludes the 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, I would like to begin with your position in the United Nations mission in Croatia. Can you please tell the Court what your job was.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Part of my job was to assist UN personnel in finding housing in the Knin area. That would entail negotiating lease terms with the landlord, and then setting up contracts with that person so a payment could be made each month to the landlord. The main bulk of my job was the accommodating of the four battle groups in Sector South: One a Canadian, one an Jordanian, a Kenyan, and a Czech Battalion. And wherever they occupied land, mostly along the Zone of Separation, I would set up the lease with the local owner of the land, so that the military could occupy that territory, and then I would bring services to those plots of land, such as electricity, water, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you or did you engage in verification of particular pieces of land or property to ensure who was the owner of that property?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It was a difficult process. The so-called owner of the land would present me with a title deed. I would then take it to the local government office that had control title deeds, and I would match it up with what they had on record to ascertain whether or not it was the real owner or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court where this government office was?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: There was only one office. It was downtown Knin, very close to what I would call the parliament building, on the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the individuals to whom you would take these titles for verification, were they civilian authorities or military?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: From your dealings with these civilian authorities, did you learn what the approximate population of Knin was in the days preceding Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes. The figure varied from 15 to 17.000 to 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you know why the figure varied so greatly between approximately 15 to 17 to 30.000?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I don't. I can make assumptions because the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if he doesn't know, I would object to any speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear on what he will base the assumptions and then perhaps see whether he has any knowledge of the facts, and then whether we should continue with the assumptions is another matter. Is there anything that apparently you made assumptions based on what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Croatian military was taking over Grahovo and coming up on the east side of Knin, there was a large swell in the population of Knin as people were leaving their local villages. So the population definitely increased dramatically. To what exact amount, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, do you know what the general makeup of this population of both people coming from other areas and in Knin in the days immediately preceding Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Women, children, old people, no fighting age males.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to talk now a bit about the fuel situation in the RSK prior to Operation Storm. What can you tell the Court regarding your knowledge of the fuel situation?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That fuel was very precious, that the black market was the only where you could purchase fuel now, and that the petrol stations were effectively closed down. You purchased your petrol by purchasing one-litre Pepsi bottles that was filled with diesel or gasoline, and the price ranged up to 20 Deutschemark per litre at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the fuel situation with any ARSK soldiers in Knin or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, did you ever have occasion to observe the condition of any ARSK tanks prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would be daily stopped at check-points throughout Sector South to -- by RSK soldiers. Usually, they would have heavy weapons to block those roads, such as old Soviet-style tanks, mostly T-55s. They would either have no petrol in them or their mechanisms for turning the turret would be probably comical at best would probably describe the situation. But on one day, they turned the turret of the their tank, it knocked the side of a building, and the actual barrel fell off the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, with respect to that last incident of the barrel falling of the tank, do you recall generally where that happened?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- the road I forget, but it was the road coming up from Vrlika to Knin. Approximately halfway along that road was the main check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court approximately how long before Operation Storm this had happened?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Within a month; shortly before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to your observations about some specific locations in Knin, and let's begin with the northern barracks. Referring to your first statement at page 2, this is also page 2 in the B/C/S translation. On that page, Mr. Dawes, you indicate that you were in the northern barracks on 3 August 1995, and I'd like to you please tell the Court whether you saw many soldiers on that date, in the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The answer to your question is I did not see many soldiers nor equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what you were doing in the northern barracks. Why did you have occasion to visit there?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: As part of my job, members of the with RSK were also land owners, and I'd have to talk to them on a monthly basis. Also, if I was going into certain areas in Sector South, I would give them a courtesy call to let them know that I was travelling there, more of a safety precaution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And referring to page 4 of that same statement, on the last paragraph of page 4, which, again, appears at the same place in the B/C/S translation, you describe taking a Serb doctor to the hospital during the shelling on 4 August. You state: "We then took the main road to the hospital. Grenades and shrapnels fell all along the road to the hospital, but not as heavy as in the centre of town. We had the top trap door of the APC open, and I was looking around. When we passed close to the northern barracks, I saw no impacts there." Mr. Dawes, can you tell the Court whether, at any later time, on either the 4th of August or afterwards, you noticed any significant shelling damage to the northern barracks itself?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I travelled passed the northern barracks many times after the morning of the 4th and saw no damage to those barracks that you could see with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to the top of page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S translation this appears at page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There you describe another trip into Knin during the shelling on 4 August where you got close to the Tvik factory and railway yards from the south. You state: "This area was totally devastated by the shelling. I did not see any military personnel or equipment in this area. The railway had not been used before, and I had been in the Tvik factory many times before the attack without seeing anything of military importance in these facilities." Now, Mr. Dawes, first, can you tell the Court why you had occasion to be inside the Tvik factory many times.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The -- what I refer to as the general manager of the screw factory was a landowner, and I would be going to him on a monthly basis to talk to him about ongoing issues with -- with land that we were leasing from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court approximately when the last time you were in that factory was?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The exact date, no; but it would have been within a month of August the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you would, please, describe for the Court exactly what it is you saw in the Tvik factory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I dealt mainly with this gentleman in his administrative part of the complex, but I never saw any activities in the warehouses, any production. It was all very quiet, like the place was not being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to be clear, did you see any soldiers or military equipment inside that factory?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned in the quote which I read that the railway had not been used before. Can you please explain to the Court how you know that.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I lived in my vehicle basically from Monday to Friday from 8.00 to 5.00 travelling, and the main supply routes throughout Sector South always paralleled railway lines. So I always travelled by the railway lines everyday, and I never saw work being done on the tracks and functioning. I never saw what you call a locomotive or a railcar, and Knin was -- is a railway town. A lot of the population would talk to me about how they had lost their income because they couldn't work anymore because the trains were not running.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to page 6 of your first statement, at the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S translation, this appears at page 6, but at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, there, you describe travelling to the ECMM headquarters during the shelling on 4 August 1995, and I would like you, please, to describe for the Court what happened in that area.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: We were travelling to the ECMM to pick them up because they'd requested to be evacuated. When we travelled down the main road, the shelling was getting less severe; and when we branched off to go done to the ECMM house off the main road, the shelling almost became what I would call targeted. We were being bracketed by what I believe was mortar rounds, some falling short, some falling over our APC; and when we dismounted from the personnel carrier, a mortar landed very close to me - I don't know exactly how close, but very close - enough to pick me up and physically move me backwards. The UN security person I was with, I remember him sort of dragging me to my feet, and then we moved into the ECMM house. I realized had I had been injured in my right ear, and then, ironically enough, the people from the ECMM house then refused to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Court why you believe that these were mortar rounds.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: They definitely were not rockets because once you have been rocketed, you'll always know the sound or you can actually see the rockets coming. It is my belief that they were mortars because of the distinct sound that they make, and -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You also mentioned that had you been bracketed. Can you please explain to the Court what that means.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Well, I was not an expert on artillery in the morning, but I certainly was quickly becoming one. They would have rounds fall short of a target and then rounds go over your head, and then they would split the difference and start shelling in the middle. And on that specific incident, the rounds were falling 40 to 50 metres short of us and then 40 to 50 metres in front of us, and then they started dropping them basically on top of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you notice this kind of bracketing fire occurring any place else in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: In the downtown core on our first trip, when we were up in the residential areas behind the parliament buildings, I could say that was where I could see it, and by the residential area by the Tvik factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just get a clarification. Is he talking about the bracketing in the morning of the 4th of mortar rounds or rounds in general, because it is very, very different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could you please seek clarification on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, the fire which you are describing in the residential area behind the parliament building and by the residential area near the Tvik factory, are you able to say whether this is mortar fire or some other kind of fire?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You did mention those two areas: Parliament building, residential area by the Tvik factory area. I don't know if you had any other areas to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: In general?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just from what you observed on the 4th or 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would say that, in general, the shelling downtown was not targeted. But when I got further outside of town, towards the ECMM building, there was definitely a sense that we were being targeted because of the shot over and shot under rounds. While we were in downtown, it was more randomly, more rocket fire. When we got to the outside of town, it was more artillery/mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 4 of your first statement, this time referring to the second-to-last paragraph on page 4, which is also the same location in the B/C/S, there you state: "After picking up the PIO and his staff, we went approximately half a kilometre north into a purely residential area, where is also situated a school. This was between 6.30 and 7.00 a.m. We then picked up approximately eight Russian and Slovakian maintenance workers. The shelling was still intense in this area. Civilian houses were hit. The school was totally destroyed which I discovered two days after." Mr. Dawes can you please tell the Court how you learned about the school being totally destroyed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It was told to me by another party, I forget the individual who's name it was, but I never laid eyes on the school. I stare directly at it after Storm was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: To be clear, when you say that the school was -- or you were told the school was totally destroyed, was that from artillery or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question, accurately. Artillery or rockets, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall identifying that particular school on a photograph during your proofing session?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5506.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at the screen, Mr. Dawes, is the building circled in red the school which we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 5506.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, could we have a date when this was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was taken in the summer of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, I take it from that concession that the right part of this roof that looks like it's a different colour does not exemplify what the roof looked like after Operation Storm on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm certainly willing to stipulate to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll accept the stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The school was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That was what the witness was told by another witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But didn't he see it after two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe the witness's testimony was that he was told that after two days, that he didn't actually observe the destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No further objections, then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P982 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, I'd now like to turn to the observations you made about burning and looting which occurred after Operation Storm. And referring to page 8 of your first statement, this would be in the third paragraph of page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S translation, this appears on page 7, also on the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, there, Mr. Dawes, you discuss the looting of Serbian property by HV soldiers which you observed and 5 August 1995, and I would like to you please describe what you saw on that day.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: We had a bird's eye view of the front gate, the Croatian armed forces had been in town for a while; and once you were observing the front gate, you could see vehicles coming by that would have personal items strapped to the top of those vehicles, inside the vehicles. I would call them high value items: TV sets, dining-room table, fridges, freezers, items like that. Vehicles that they were driving in would have KN registered licence plates, so Knin registered licence plates. The people occupying the vehicles were Croatian. You could tell by the type of uniform they were wearing and their shoulder flashes with the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Court whether or not these soldiers that you saw carrying these items were drunk or sober?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The mood was quite festive on the Croatian side. They were celebrating the win of Knin. There was a good number of Croatian soldiers that were openly intoxicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, just for my understanding about the school, there might have been some confusion. You were told two days later that the school had been destroyed. You never observed it yourself after this was told to you? You've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, with regard to the looting which you observed outside the compound on the 5th, can you tell the Court whether you observed any HV commanders or officers rank present during this looting?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if an HV commander had been present, would what you observed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, this is pure speculation, if an HV commander had been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait for the question. It started with an assumption, which doesn't necessarily mean that the whole of the question would be speculative as well. Mr. Russo, could you phrase your question and, Mr. Dawes, could you wait to answer that question until I've given permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, if an HV commander had been present, would what you observed on the 5th of August outside the compound have been noticeable to, in fact, anyone in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Judge, it is of no consequence given what the Chamber is looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking whether he could see it? Yes. I take it that if you're in the right place to see it, then you can see it. If you are behind a wall or behind a building, then you couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ... [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if commanders were there, it's of vital importance for the answer to the question where they were. And if they were in the right place, if you can see something, everyone who is not blind can see it as well, if he is just in the right position. You would agree with that, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would agree with that specific point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please explore further what the witness is tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, what you observed outside the compound on the 5th of August, was it isolated to a very small place or was it occurring over a relatively large area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, if I may, from based on what he could see inside the base, the UN base, I assume that, just by way of clarification, that's what he is asking: What the witness could see when he was in the base on the 5th, which he never left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's what you're asking exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness to answer the question based on what he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let me just look at the question again: "What you observed outside the compound on the 5th of August, was it isolated." Perhaps the witness could, in his answer, also include from what position he was able to see what, and then, in this context, answer the question whether it was isolated to a very small place or occurring over a relatively large area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, just by one point of clarification, the evidence that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear the answer of the witness, and then if there's any need to put further questions. Please, Mr. Dawes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a map of the camp would be great for you right now, sir, so you could actually se it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a map in front much us. You have a map marked, and this one is attached to your second statement. So we have that map available, and we have some familiarity with the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. So the front gate where I was located and the main administrative buildings that would overlook the road that would -- was in right in front of the camp, Your Honour, I noticed that that road was full, and the parking lot that was across the main gate was full of personal belongs from houses, like TV sets, dining-room tables, et cetera, and that the Croatian soldiers were handling those pieces of equipment. That's directly what I saw from that advantage point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In front of the main gate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The -- further down on that same page, page 8 of your first statement, Mr. Dawes, you discuss a trip that you took outside the UN camp on 6 August, and you indicate that you went through the village of Vrbnik. I'd like to you please describe for the Court what you witnessed happening in Vrbnik.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: When you leave the main -- sorry. When you leave the main camp, you take a direct left, you go to the top of the hill. As soon as you get to the top of the hill, there's an intersection. At that intersection, there was some dead civilian bodies. And on that road, once you hang a right, there were Croatian soldiers that were openly looting houses along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I don't know if your answer was specific to Vrbnik or not, but I wanted to know what you saw in the town of Vrbnik, not along the way. Of course, your answer is fine with respect to that. I'm not sure if you were answering in Vrbnik or on the way to Vrbnik.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: In Vrbnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether or not you saw any houses either burning or being destroyed in the town of Vrbnik.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The houses had already been destroyed and the contents of the houses had been remove to the sides of the roads or into the back of different vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Dawes, were you able to tell whether there were any -- well, first, let me ask you: Who was doing the looting?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The specific unit of the HV, I'm not sure; but they were Croatian soldiers. I can quantify that by -- Croatian soldiers are very different from RSK soldiers. They were always properly attired, very much in full regalia with beret, flak vest, uniforms, carry their weapons properly, very organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you able to determine whether there were any HV commanders present in the town of Vrbnik on 6 August.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing anybody in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving to the next page of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This would be in the B/C/S translation at the bottom of page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicate that you moved on to visit the town of Kistanje, and, again, I would like you to describe for the Court what you observed happening in Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: May I take a second to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: So, after leaving Vrbnik, we followed on that road, got to Kistanje, I would say, half an hour later. There was many more soldiers in Kistanje than there was in Vrbnik, I would say a company size in total. Again, they were wearing their normal HV uniforms, and they were actively looting and sacking the town of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what the term "sacking" means to you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: They were taking the personal belongs of people -- sorry, they taking the personal belongs out of the houses and putting them into either the back of army vehicles or personal vehicles or storing them on the sides of road for later pick-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether you noticed any destruction of buildings or burning happening in that town.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes. The town was being destroyed. Some houses would not be destroyed, and the -- they would either put a symbol on those houses identifying it as a Croatian house. The remainder of the houses would be destroyed, and I would - nobody likes hearing the word "assume" - but I'd assume those would be Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, again, did you take note or happen to notice if there were in the HV commanders present in Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Such a large group of soldiers, again you would assume there would be a commander; but I don't remember seeing one or talking to one on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, following on to the middle of page 9 in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This appears in the B/C/S translation at the top of page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicate that on the way back to Knin on this trip, you came to an intersection on the route to Srb, and I would like you to explain to the Court what it was that you saw at that intersection?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: There were a group of people who had been killed. They were laying on the left side of the road, if you were driving to Knin, right by the Srb exist; S-r-b exit, I mean. There was battle damage to their vehicles, and they were dead and they had been dead for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you say "battle damage," can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The civilian vehicles were showing signs of splay damage, shrapnel damage, and small-arms fire to the vehicle. I didn't identify how the victims died. We didn't get out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether you could see or whether you were able to make a determination as to whether these were civilian people or military?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: More specifically and clarification of how they were dressed, not whether they were civilian or military, but how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could explore that in cross-examination. How did they appear to you and perhaps you explain why they appear to you as either military or civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We will they were not all males. There was a combination of females to male. The females were definitely not in uniform. The males, it is a difficult question. May I have time to explain it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please explain as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Republic of Serbian Krajina, any fighting-age male was deemed part of the armed forces, Your Honour, and normal Serbian attire would dictate that they would have a piece of camouflage clothing on them. So it was not uncommon to see civilians dressed with camouflage trousers. The people that -- the males that I saw dead that specific incident, some of them did have camouflage trousers on, but they had civilian tops. They did not have any rank or insignia on them, and there was no weapons around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Dawes, can you say approximately how many people you saw dead at that intersection.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: To the exact number, no. There were a bunch of dead people, more than 15, less than 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicate in your statement that later on, on the way back from that trip, you were able to make it through the town of Knin itself, and I would like you to describe for the Court what you witnessed in Knin on that day.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: When we left that area, approximately three kilometres from the outskirts of Knin, on the outskirts of Knin, we were stopped by a Croatian military police check-point. They asked us for identification, they did a radio -- they talked on the radios for a couple of minutes, and then they allowed us through the town. We stopped immediately at the other person in the vehicle, who was driving with me, at his place to pick up personal belongings. His house had been looted. Then we continued down the main street of Knin, directly all the way downtown, back to the barracks. Driving through the town of Knin on that morning or afternoon was the first time I saw Knin after the dust had settled, so to speak. The house -- the house. The town was full of Croatian military, Croatian police, and the -- the town was being cleaned, garbage was being piled, personal belongings were being piled. It was a surreal experience. There was mountains of belongings on the sides of the roads as government or people from the armed forces were emptying the apartment blocks and the houses of all their personal belongings. There was a horrible smell in the town, and we saw a lot of hazmat people cleaning obviously the contents of fridges since the power had been off. We saw dead bodies being removed from houses. We saw -- I saw organised dismantling of a town from a personal belongings point of view, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to separate out a limited of what you've said. First of all, with respect to the removal of personal belongings from apartments, can you tell the Court how these belongings were being handled. Were they being separated in any way, all thrown out, anything you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Items of no interest at all would be thrown out balconies to pile on the street below. Items of value would be carried down, and they would be separated into different piles. So there would be a pile of TV sets, there would be a pile of stereos, there would be a pile of fridges et cetera, et cetera. Then the garbage would be -- or the items of non-value would be put into backs of trucks and taken away, and items of value were put in the back of lorries. That's what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And your use of the term "organised," the organised dismantling of a town, can you explain to the Court what you mean by "organised"?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: If I may use Vrbnik and Kistanje as an example of non-organised, i.e., a bunch of soldiers that were not placing items in different piles that were just -- I guess, I like to use the word "rabble" or a unorganised bunch of people. Knin was very systematic. It was very organised in the sense that items from the town were being stockpiled into different piles, and there was definitely a sense of -- of order. Some groups of people were doing certain tasks, other people doing different tasks. It was very much like a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on that same page of your first statement, Mr. Dawes - and this appears at the bottom of page 8 on the B/C/S - you mention a trip that you took on 8 August along the Knin-Drnis road, and I would like you to please explain for the Court what you observed happening along that road.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Because of the amount of refugees we had in our camp, we needed potable drinking water. The only source of potable drinking water was in the coast, Croatia. We had to travel to Primosten to pick up water in bowzer. I was tasked with doing that job. So we had to travel on that road to Drnis, which is again a half-hour drive from Knin; and along that way, there would be different check-points on the road by Croatian forces, never policija, always armed forces, always military. And along that road, there are a lot of small villages either directly on the road or indented by up to half a kilometre but visible from the road. And when we drove in on the morning to get the water, very professional Croatian military unit - I've never seen them before or after - spoke good English, the people at the check-points. They wanted to see our identifications and what we were doing. They were satisfied with what we were up to. Then, if you looked past the check-point, i.e., to the sides of the road, you could see that in the morning time, they were again systematically removing the contents from people's houses and storing them either besides the houses or in the back of -- of Croatian military trucks. You can tell a designation of the -- you can tell they were of military vehicles because the licence plates started with HV, Hrvatska Vojska. We travelled -- sorry. There was also good command and control. The persons at the check-point didn't know what to do with us, so he called for his higher, and a - I don't know the Croatian rank on the structure - but a person of rank and authority came to the vehicle; you can tell by their demeanour. He spoke to me and asked me what I was up to, and he then gave me permission to travel along the road. We went and got the water along the coast and came back later in the afternoon, and those same villages that they were looting, they were now burning and the skyline was black. You needed to have your headlights on. The dirt and dust and the crap from the houses burning was blowing across the road, and that was, without exaggeration, from Drnis to Knin. Most villages along that road were completely destroyed on that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dawes, do you recall drawing on a map the routes that you travelled on both 5th August and 6th August?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we please have 65 ter 5505.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Dawes, I'm going to ask to you briefly explain to the Court the routes, which ones represent which day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could move to sort of the middle bottom there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, if you would, please, explain to the Court what these routes represent.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The circular route was the route that I went through Vrbnik, Kistanje, and then back to Knin; and the up and down route, north to south route, was the route that I used to get to Drnis that day to get the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Could I please have that admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P983, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P983 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, and for the benefit of the Bench and for Defence counsel, I have provided demonstrative, digitally-enhanced photographs that actually indicate in larger print the names of the towns passed through on this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, do you also recall marking, on an aerial photograph of Knin, the locations of some of the buildings and areas referenced in your two statements?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5504.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, do you recognise this as the aerial for upon which you made those markings?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would like to have 65 ter 5504 admitted into evidence. The letters indicated on here are all explained in the second statement of Mr. Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Russo, we got a map on our desk. That appears not to be the same, although the markings are quite similar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was also provided, just as an aid to the Court, a digitally-enhanced version of what you now see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I liked very much, as a matter of fact, was that the contrasting colours on the map on our desk, for the first time, I really could see what is marked and what is the map. Now, is there any reason has the witness marked it twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It is not a marking twice by the witness, Your Honour. We simply took the aerial photograph which had been marked by the witness and digitally enhanced the drawings on our own as an aid to the Court. We can certainly, if the Defence counsel has no objection, we can certainly have the digitally-enhanced portions uploaded to replace P983 and 65 ter 5504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no objection. It seems looking to me, just looking at the digitally-enhanced photograph, that it reflects what is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to me, but, of course, it always takes me sometime to always carefully compare, whether what we've got in front of us is the same as we see on the screen, rather than to have two different versions. It very much looks to be the same. Now this, what we have on the screen now, is the map marked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are we supposed to work from that one or from this better legible one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I thought I would leave it to the Court's preference. I simply provided the digitally-enhanced one in case, when these are uploaded, they're quite difficult to look at on e-court, so I thought a hard copy might be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the one is in evidence, and the other is not. That is, well, I couldn't say is bothering me that much, but it is the same, could we have the best one in evidence, so if later we use it. If the parties agree they are the same, then, Mr. Russo, you are invited to upload into e-court the one which gives the best possibilities of seeing what accurately was marked, and you may have noticed that I made comments on this at some previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We already have a map marked by the witness, and perhaps, after the break, you'll inform us whether it will be the one which is uploaded now or whether it will be replaced by the digitally-enhanced copy. Mr. Registrar, the map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number P984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P984 is admitted into evidence. And if you want to replace it by the digitally-enhanced copy, then we'd like to hear from you, Mr. Russo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, after the Croatians took over Knin, did you continue in your responsibilities as an accommodations officer?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what was left for you to do with respect to apartments and property used by UN employees?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Both UN civilian properties and military properties were still being used, so since there were no new landlords in town, I had to set up the exact same boiler plate contracts between the new Croatian landlords and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you follow the same process of verifying ownership for the new Croatian landlords?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: We did. It was the exact same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you the tell the Court whether it was done out of the same office as had been done for the RSK authorities?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court what this verification of the Croatian landowner property, do you know whether or not it came from the same paperwork? Were you able to determine whether it was the same paperwork that the Croats had which the RSK had had?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, it was different -- different deeds. The reason why you'd know this is that on some part of the land deed, there would actually be a stamp of -- so, for example, the Croatian stamp would have the chequer-board down in the corner, and it would be in Croatian. The with RSK deed would have the -- I believe it is the eagle of the RSK, and it would be in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no further question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Kehoe, we could take an earlier break and then ask you to start. It depends if you have a subject which could be covered in some ten minutes then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I really do, Judge. I have a quick subject that I can get through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Dawes you will now cross-examined first by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dawes. Just looking at P983, again, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, uploading of maps usually takes some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, this is the map that we just talked about previously. Who was with you when you made this trip, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I was with another UN employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: A security officer for the UN, Andries Dreyer, I believe was his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you took this trip with Andries Dreyer?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for interrupting, but I'm asking for clarification on which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two trips represented on the map, and that has been covered in direct examination. The circle represents the 6th, the straight line represents the 8th. I'm simply asking Mr. Kehoe to clarify which trip he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, if the witness has a question about clarification, the witness should ask. Counsel should not be rising to instruct the witness on how to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe intervened several times, asking that Mr. Russo be more precise and make distinctions, which logically follow from the previous testimony of the witness. You asked about "this trip," Mr. Kehoe, where the witness clearly explained the map giving the itinerary of two trips. Mr. Russo is fully entitled to ask you to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, emotions seem to be rather Friday-like, than Monday morning-like. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You took a trip on the 6th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where did you go on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That was the one to Vrbnik, Kistanje, back to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that is the circle?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The circle route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was with you then?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Andries Dreyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what type of vehicle were you driving?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: An UN mini-van.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what was the date of the next trip?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe it is the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is the trip that you have going south to Drnis?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was with you then?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I was driving in an UN vehicle, an SUV, by myself; and then we would have the lorry drivers or the truck drivers were in my convoy. I don't know how many or who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So how many vehicles where were with you going down towards Drnis?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Two or three, don't know exactly the amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you were by yourself in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That I can remember. There may have been somebody else with me. I -- I can't remember on that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it against UN policy for you to be driving alone?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's misleading. It is against in some areas, but as long as you have people in a convoy with you, you're not technically along. So depending on the threat level, it would indicate whether or not you can travel alone or not. I'm not sure of the threat level on the 8th, but I may have had been with -- by myself or had somebody with me. But there was definitely other UN people in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, who else was in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: We have specific people who would be allowed to drive lorries, and they would be those people, UN civilians, international workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you have any names?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how many UN people were in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Again, I'm not trying to defer the answer. I just can't remember how many people were with me. Two or three, four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there any members of the United Nations military police, a military police contingent from the United Nations as part of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there was no military whatsoever here.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you remember Captain Geoff Hill?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe he was the OC of the Canadian -- sorry, UN military police detachment in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was Mr. Hill, Captain Hill, with you on this trip on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know Captain Phil Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The name is not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to P962. Let me cover a few quick matters before the break -- P62, excuse me, P62.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speakers to make a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As this map is coming up, as you can see, Mr. Dawes, this is a map of Knin; and with the assistance of the usher, and just referring back to your statements where you said you took three trips out on the 4th of August, I would like you to, with the assistance of the usher, draw the route that you took on your first trip on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Sorry. I've never used one of these before. You just literally do what you're supposed to do, I imagine, right? Okay, I got it. I'm sorry if I've not getting literally the street or if I'm bisecting a house right now. It's a little bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, should this have been in blue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dawes, you may not be aware of our colour codes. I think Defence was blue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think so, Judge. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no problems with blue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it's an issue of whether or not we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It gives us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think if we just remove this and start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering whether we could not also zoom in. I do not know, of course, exactly what we're covering, what itineraries. We have now only small portion of the map. It's more difficult to find your routes if it is not enlarged. Mr. Kehoe, I take it you have a better idea on where the witness is you expect him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's perhaps forget about this one. If I wouldn't mind, Mr. Dawes, that you will be invited to do the same again for the second time, where perhaps we can zoom in on that portion of the map which finally will make it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, I think there is quite a bit drawing. That's why I went large first, Judge, then we can zoom in from where he puts the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that we can't, once marking starts, we can't change the zoom level anymore. So we have to do it right from the beginning to find the right part of the picture, then invite the witness to mark. If you could perhaps guide in finding the right portion of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Should I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, I'd like to have the lower right part enlarged, then that is what, then, will be done, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is actually his route on the first trip, I believe, is going to cover from the left-hand side all the way -- by the hospital back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we need the whole of the map, you would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the witness to do as good as he can, but now with the blue marker. Madam Usher, could you assist? The witness has the marker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been changed to blue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map is empty now, there is no markings on it any more, and you're invited to make the markings Mr. Kehoe asks you in blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first trip out was quite complex. Am I allowed to read my statement first and then draw?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. Just use anything you'd need to assist you along.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Forgive me if I missed a street by a block or two. It's the general area that I went that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you've returned back to the UN base?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was with you on that first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, this will be totally incomprehensible for those who look at this map later. So what the witness marked, how he left UN compound on the southern part of the map, then made his way into town, passing the helicopter pad, I think; then instead of following the main road along the railway complex, he turned a little bit to the west, then to the north again, then to the east, where he apparently came to the place where you can cross the railways; then he made, in north-easterly direction, his way in the direction of the hospital, the last portion being south-easterly and then north-easterly again. Then he returned from the hospital, same route, exactly up to where the railway bridge is; there he then moved in south-easterly direction, along the Tvik complex; then last portion moving in northerly direction. There where the marking stops, he apparently turned, made his way again in southerly direction for a small distance; then going into a north-westerly direction again to the place where the railways can be crossed; and then made, after having crossed the railway, made back his way to the UN compound in the same way apparently as he had come, that is, not following the main road along the railway complex, but moving a little bit into a westerly direction, then back south, a little east again, and then further following the main road to the UN compound. That is what I understood the marking to be, because, otherwise, if you later look at this picture, you would not know where he went because did he not explain it in words. You would agree that this is approximately what you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And going back to the question, who was with you on this first trip?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't accurately identify the people that were in the vehicle with me. I know I was in a Jordanian APC, that the crew commander was Jordanian and the driver was Jordanian in my APC. I'm not sure if Andries Dreyer was in another APC behind me or if he was in the same APC as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer this into evidence, as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D855 is admitted into evidence. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can take the break now. I mean, I was going to have two quick things to do, but I don't know. It's going to be a similar exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dreyer [sic], if you could turn to your 1996 statement at P980, page 3, last paragraph. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Page 3 in my original statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Good to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Last paragraph, second sentence: "Andries Dreyer was in one APC, I was in the second one, This was my first trip downtown this morning," and it says, "Dreyer and the clerk had been down before."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Top of the page, page 4, there's a call to the Chief of Staff to go and pick up a Jordanian colonel. The first -- second full sentence: "I then joined the first APC where Andries Dreyer was, and the second APC went to pick up the colonel, and we continued on the main road into Knin." Does that refresh your recollection that you were with Andries Dreyer for your first trip?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: A little bit, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go and put up another copy of P62 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Dawes, with the assistance of the usher, if you could draw the route you took on your second trip on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I do believe we have to put that back to its original size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, using the blue pencil, if you could draw that second trip.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It's blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I return the same way. Do you want me to leave it that way so I don't make it with another parallel line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The marking started at the UN compound, went then into an easterly direction, bending to southerly direction where it meets the limits of the map, and you came back on the same road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Came back on the same road --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If there could just one clarifying on that score, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the direction when you went towards the village of Potkonje. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. I went back to the main camp, and then we started off on the -- I guess it would be part B of the second trip, if you want to refer to it as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, second part of the marking is leaving again from the UN compound, taking the main road into town; now following the road along the railway complex, crossing the railway, going into south-easterly direction, and turning to the left, making a kind of a circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then following back the same direction, back to the camp, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Joining the road where the witness went, then going back to where he crossed the railway, and then going the same way back, the main road, to the UN compound. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Andries Dreyer was with you on this trip as well, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to page 5 of P980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before I do, Your Honour, I would like to tender the photograph on the screen with Mr. Dawes's markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D856.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D856 is admitted into evidence. I heard you say D -- yes, D856. Initially, it appeared as "D956," but D856 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the second-to-last paragraph of page 5, talking about your second trip: "However, instead of going downtown immediately, we decided to go to Potkonje to the UNMO station. On this trip, Engleby," should be Sergeant Engleby, "was also with us." Now, who is the "us"?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That would be the crew of the APC. I wasn't driving the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back, is part of the "us," Mr. Dreyer?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us, once again, put up a copy of P62.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Dawes, the same exercise, if could you just draw, using blue, your third trip, the route that you took.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Sorry. My blue pen has entered the barracks. I didn't mean for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
