utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist the witness in erasing a portion of -- Meanwhile, I describe the marking made until now; that is, leaving the UN compound, taking the main road to the city, crossing the Krka river, taking the main road along halo, following the railway complex, crossing the railway; and then to continue a road following the railway, not going into the town, the road which leads to -- or follows going to the western -- passing on the western side the barracks. Then you return the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I said "passing the barracks," which are the northern barracks, I have to correct that. It stops approximately when the road has reached the barracks, and then returning along the railway road, crossing the railway road, and then taking the same way back to the UN compound. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I can continue drawing my trip on the third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, then there was a mistake. I thought you had returned. So we are now at the western side of what is called the northern barracks, from what I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I retraced my steps back to the roundabout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The roundabout where you can cross the railway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then I travelled by the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now something appears on the screen which looks like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looks like I need some more administrative help, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher or Mr. Registrar, do you know how to get rid of ... We apparently do not know how to get rid of this ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I say it in words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. If you do it slowly, then we can -- Is there no way to continue the marking? Let's see whether our technicians are able to help us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we get rid of this and try to do the exercise again, which might be more clear. Mr. Registrar, could we have a clean P62 on the screen. Mr. Dawes, you're invited to start again at the UN compound and do the marking as you did it before and then to continue. Yes. Madam Usher, could you assist Mr. Dawes getting rid of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not on purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I know. One second. Madam Usher will help you. We're now on the map where it reads "Knin army BKS."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I travelled back to the main roundabout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and then I returned by the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first describe. From the roundabout, you took the road in north-westerly direction, passing the -- I should say north-easterly direction, passing the northern barracks on the eastern side, and then continuing; and, there, where the marking stops, you returned and took the same road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, to the roundabout again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is now in a south-westerly direction, up to the point of the roundabout where you can pass the railway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I'll take over from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There, you took the road in south-easterly direction, which bends then to north-easterly direction, and then a right turn. You then ended up in an area with some larger structures; and from there, you returned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to the camp, so same route back to the roundabout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- same route; that is, same route back to the roundabout, crossing the railway, following the railway complex, and then taking the route back to the UN compound. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we can offer this map with the markings on it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes D857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D857 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, this was the trip where you said that you were at the ECMM house where the mortar shelling was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is the ECMM house?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It's in that general area where I sort of stopped marking. It's in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mean in the area by the -- by the northern barracks?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Past the northern barracks, well down that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you circle the approximate area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was Mr. Dreyer with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe he was, but I can't guarantee that. I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, who was the UN person that you said that took you into the UN [sic] house?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Which UN house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, the ECMM house. You noted directly this morning that when the mortar attack took place, one UN person took you into the ECMM house. Who was that UN person?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe it was Andries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And using this photograph and the markings, you cannot circle in the general direction where the ECMM house is?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Down that road, on the left-hand side someplace. That's about as best as I can do for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "down that road, on the left-hand side," are you referring to the road that goes to the west side of the northern barracks?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm never very good with a map. I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... north similar to the left?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It's the route that goes past the hospital, the blue route that I traced past the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's where I said that he passed the eastern part of the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, let me just turn away from this for a second, and I had attempted to go through this exercise prior to court today. You were in contact with the Gotovina Defence prior to coming to The Hague to meet with you to discuss these matter, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Are you talking about the one that happened a couple of years ago in Calgary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about recent e-mail traffic with Mr. Stanton?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Is that Mike there? It's been a couple of years. Yeah, that's correct. He contacted me approximately a week ago, maybe longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you informed him at that time that you were willing to meet the Gotovina Defence when you got to The Hague. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe that I said I would be in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But when the request came to talk to you within the latter part of last week, you declined?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you discuss that with members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: They didn't tell me either way. They just said that I had a right to see the Defence counsel if I wished to seem them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, when you told Mr. Stanton prior to coming here that you would be in contact, what did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That either party would try and reach out and touch base with each other before the trial started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I chose not to do that, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And why was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I had just finished a seven-month tour in Afghanistan, and my wife met me in Holland and I had over things on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You did meet with the Office of the Prosecutor, though.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct, to go over my statement that I made in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object to the relevance of this. I believe the witness has already indicated that he didn't want to talk and why. I'm not sure what the benefit of going into any more of this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I find it somewhat remarkable that on -- and we can do this outside of the presence of the witness because this is it not an isolated witness, and I brought it to the attention of the Prosecutor. This is not the first instances where this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not discuss it in the presence of the witness. The witness has explained why he has chosen not to meet with you. I'm not encouraging you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further deal with the matter. Although, of course, I do not know what you have in your mind, so I'm not keeping you off strictly, but the guidance may be clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, from your statement, you got to the area in May of 1994. And when you had arrived there, there had already been a huge displacement of Croats, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, approximately, how many Croats did you learn had been displaced from the Krajina when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would not know the figure. I would know it to be a large figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you talking about thousands and thousands?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, virtually all of the young Croats had left the Krajina, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear Mr. Kehoe. Please speak into the microphone. Thank you. I know it's far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the first time I have been accused of not being heard, Judge. It's taken me back a bit, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take care that it doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, by the time you got there, virtually all of the Croat houses had been destroyed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were there prior to Operation Storm, were any of the UN personnel taking any steps to find out who was responsible for the destruction of those Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would not know personally myself, but I would definitely make the assumption that, yes, that would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any reports on that score?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Just what I would read in the news, nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you also were travelling through the Krajina prior to Operation Storm, you noted that the churches in the Croat villages were destroyed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the destroyed churches included the churches in -- or the Catholic church in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just turn your attention to your observations to the actual people in the Krajina, the Serbs, and this is prior to Operation Storm? Is it accurate to say that virtually the entire Krajina Serb population was armed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would say that fighting age males were armed. I never saw women carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And fighting age men went from 18 to almost 60, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Dawes, going through, it was difficult for you to know, looking at a Serb, whether or not that person was a civilian or was in the ARSK because of the clothing that they wore.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes and no, if I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: You're right, in general, that male Serbs, even when they weren't on the front line, they were ordered to carry weapons with them because they were part of the militia; but, usually, the ones that weren't carrying weapons and didn't have on a full combat dress were, they usually civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you were saying that the civilians were carrying weapons -- these individuals, excuse me, carrying weapons walking around, they were walking around town with their AK-47s?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the population in the Krajina, it's a fact, is it not, that you, when you were living in Knin, had a neighbour who had an anti-aircraft weapon on his patio, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Describe this -- describe this weapon for us?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Twin-barrelled anti-aircraft weapon, probably around a 20-millimetre-type that you would sit in. It would have the arms is what I would call them, where you could move it in a 360 direction. Usually, when the Serbs won a football game or a basketball game, he would light it up at night. That was the only anti-aircraft weapon I saw in Knin, and that was my neighbours house, if I could point to the map of Knin, by the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, using this P62 that is on the screen, could you circle that, please.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Sure. I want to get this right. Approximately in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you're circling an area on the left-hand side of the road, north of -- on the road west of the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Bad with directions, again. That's basically where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was that where you lived or is that where this anti-aircraft weapon was?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Both. Just so you know, I didn't live there the whole time. When I first moved to Knin, that was the first house I lived in; and after a couple of months, I left that residence; no water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer this item into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For those who are trying to find the marking, it's in the middle of the map, small blue circle, to the northern edge of the map. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Apologies, again, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D858 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dawes, you mentioned that your neighbour fired it at football games. He also fired it at aircraft that were passing over head, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It is an anti-aircraft weapon, so I would probably say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did he not fire it at drones that were flying about the area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That was standard protocol for the Serbs to fire at drones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me just shift gears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We heard about what was standard procedure. Did you ever see this happen? Did you ever hear this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you told us "this is the only anti-aircraft weapon," this is the only anti-aircraft weapon in the area that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk for a bit about some of the items that are in your statement. Now, in your statement -- actually, in your testimony, you were talking about the black market for petrol. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How large was this black market in the Krajina prior to Operation Storm; do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do have an idea. The black market was the real economy in the Krajina, in the sense that if you wanted to purchase luxury goods, patrol, tobacco, items like that, you would purchase them on the black market. You wouldn't purchase them in a shop; you would buy them on the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, from your experience - and correct me if I'm wrong - from your experience, it was a large organised crime element in the Krajina prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I wouldn't know of that. I guess, is your definition of selling things on the black market criminal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about the black market, that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: The standard protocol to buy fuel is on the back market, so that would make them criminals, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you include the theft of UN vehicles as part of this black market?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- yes, it was an industry to steal UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the theft of these vehicles was quite prevalent, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many times did it happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Three or four times, in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, on three or four occasions in Sector South, you had UN vehicles taken from you by Krajina Serbs at gunpoint, I trust?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Definitely at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then taken to another location, to be disposed of in some fashion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I only saw one of my vehicles later on that was driven by a Serb in town, so I don't know what they did with them. The rumour has it that they go to Bosnia for a re- haul, i.e., paint them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, these people, these individuals that were stealing these vehicles and sending them to Bosnia to have them repainted, were they part of a criminal organised crime element in the area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't know if it was organised or not. I just know that it was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was there -- were there any occasions, Mr. Dawes, where UN personnel allowed their vehicles to be taken in return for money?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the automobiles, there was the instance you mentioned about fuel. Now, was that particular dissemination of fuel in the black market, was that organised?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Let's be specific. Where there was once petrol stations in Knin, they didn't fill up the big tanks anymore. They filled up them in small Pepsi bottles, and sold them in outside the gas pumps. So that is the type of what you refer to as black market fuel, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir, you referred to black market fuel this morning in direct examination with Mr. Russo. I'm just using the words that you used approximately an hour and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That fuel was sold at the petrol stations. I could mark it on the map for you, if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that's the black market that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, you lived in the area for sometime prior to Storm, as we -- as noted in your statement. We need not go into all of the details. But you were in contact with the ARSK governmental authorities on a regular basis, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, they had a degree of -- or they had a high degree of involvement in the properties that you leased for UN personnel. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They had -- they had authority over what local staff was hired by the UN, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That was a rumour. I don't know yes or no to that answer [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show D1, Defence exhibit D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just go to the first page, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, this is the agreement between the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the United Nations on the status of the UN Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dealing with UNPROFOR facilities, paragraph 13: "The RSK government shall charge UNPROFOR, in agreement with the forces command, provide premises for the headquarters, camp," et cetera, "that may be needed to carry out UNPROFOR operative and administrative activities, and for accommodation of UNPROFOR members." I realize this is UNPROFOR, not UNCRO --

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I understand what UNPROFOR is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All right. Was this the operative agreement that you were -- that you were using in your dealings with the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I guess I could start with my rank in the UN would be of like a corporal. I have never seen this document before. This would be something that the higher ups would be looking at. I followed direction from my boss in Zagreb on how we implemented land lease transactions. I have never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And realizing that you have never seen it before, let me ask you about the contents once we read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could turn to paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That first sentence, if you could read it for us, Mr. Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Of 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR shall engage local staff that they need only through the government agency for commercial relations with international organisations, and agreement ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you want the witness to read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No problem with that, but also when you start reading, speed of speech goes up, so if you read it just for yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it was fine that you read it. It was either me reading or you reading. It was perfectly okay.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Good to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that particular sentence, were you aware that the UNPROFOR, the UN, had to hire local staff through the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I was not, and nor did I hire any staff. They were all hired by the time I got there, local staff in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, were you aware that the RSK was using local staff to gather intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a report from the General Staff of the ARSK, talking about Operation Action or Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, earlier I have expressed the view of the Chamber that witnesses are here to tell what you say they know and not to be educated. Of course, if you have any reasonable ground to believe that if a witness sees a document, that suddenly something will come into his mind on the matter on which he said before that he didn't know anything about it, then, of course, if there's a reasonable ground to believe that that will happen, we'll let you go. But, at the same time, let's not put to the witness the evidence of things he apparently doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my question, Judge, is some of the content and identification of individuals I would like to inquire of the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, then, of course, the easiest way is to first ask him whether a name ranges bell; and then if he says, yes, then, of course, you can put another document to him, not the other way around. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is a document, sir, from the security department of the ARSK. In the first sentence, it says: "The UNPROFOR translator in southern barracks (department of civilian affairs), a certain Jelena (most likely Pribojan) for reasons unknown, revealed to our source information that the HV was going to conduct aggression against the RSK ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, it continues concerning comments made by Jelena.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then, once again, on the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, talking about Jelena in the second paragraph. Now, Mr. Dawes, do you know this women, Jelena?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, that is exactly the question I would have expected you to ask first, whether he knew of any translator by the name of Jelena, because then we could have skipped all of this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are some other items in these documents that I would like do ask the witness about just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But, again, let's see what the witness can tell us. Let's not take him through a whole story and then ask him, "Did you know the person?" "No, I didn't know the person." So please keep this in mind. I asked to you do this two minutes ago; nevertheless, you continued with the document instead of putting the first question: "Do you know any translator by the name of ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... understand, Judge. I understand. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you say you understand, but, apparently, I have to explain it to you twice before you really understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was some content in the document that I wanted to address, and I'm going to into in detail right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, on the third paragraph of this page, it talks about setting up a signalling system from inside the Sector South base. During your stay at UN Sector South, did you become aware of that in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going down to the bottom of this page on the insert that says "the 13th of November," it notes the Jordanian battalion was replaced with the Canadian battalion, and this indicates a better possibility of cooperation. Do you have any idea, based on your significant time at UN Sector South, why the ARSK would believe that there would be better cooperation in detailing with the Canadians than dealing with the Jordanian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm going to object to the foundation of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if we understand the question to be that Mr. Kehoe would like to know whether the witness is acquainted with any fact which could explain this expectation in the RSK, then the witness can answer. Is that what your question was about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will -- since the witness does not who the individual is, I will at the appropriate time bar table some other documents on that score, and don't need to address them at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we suggested a procedure for bar table that we would know at least what it is about, because since the witness cannot tell us anything about the documents is, as such, not great information for us to see whether they should accept it or not. But I think we made suggestions earlier on how to deal with bar table documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to moving on, though, I will move into evidence across bar table 1D57-0017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was what? Because I don't have--

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is the document -- the three-page document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D859 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could turn our attention to 1D57-0023.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now that I have actually read the document and instructions on the signal board --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and I have read the actual contents, the UN has, for each camp it operates, has a different threat assessment for what state of threat we are in currently. I forget the specifics of it, but basically green/good, red/bad. That -- those flags would flutter each day to what threat level our internal camp was at, with regards to aggression from the RSK. So instructions on the signal board, I'm just reading it now and it is obvious that that's our own UN interpretation of the local threat level in Knin, either airborne threat, ground threat, what's the general mood of Sector South, not necessarily a nefarious act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say what you read here, apparently those who drafted the document understood what your signalling system was and which was publicly displayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, did you publicly disclose your signalling system to the RSK government on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would not know. I'm not part of the military. The only thing I know is that at the front of the each camp in the UN, we would have a standard signalling board, where we would show that the vehicles going out of the camp would what threat level they were going into, and it was a flag system based on colour-coded flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And by the way, what was that threat level op the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It was dark. I don't know. I wasn't at the front gate at 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you know what the threat level was between 3.45 and 5.00?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to another document, 1D57-0023.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a report from the 2nd of December involving Plavana, who in the other documents is identified as Jelena Pribojan. If we could look at the second page that mentions you, Mr. Dawes, this is at the 2nd of December. Notes a meeting with Agent Plava. Second paragraph: At approximately 1100 hours in the office of the agent, Murray Dawes entered," another translator was present," and said: 'Croatians have concentrated significant forces throughout the whole of Dalmatia, and are planning to bring in new forces, pack your children, and go to Belgrade with your family. You will surely be attacked within the next two or three days.'" Now, Mr. Dawes, first, were you authorised in the UN to transmit military information to the civilian personnel in UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't have a security clearance in the UN. I was -- I don't pass military information on. I'm not part of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you see before you an item where you are identified by name entering the office of the agent, who is identified in the other documents as Jelena Pribojan. Did you pass this information on to the local staff?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would not believe so. I wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go down to the next paragraph, and you see the next name, Kmetic Igor; Igor Kmetic. Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I believe I do. He is a translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know anything about him and his family?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what do you know?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: He was an UN translator whose father was ex-JNA, and they lived in Knin during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have contact with that family when you -- when they -- or did they come into UN Sector South headquarters after the 4th or 5th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct. They were refugees in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have contact with the father during that time?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 1D57-0023.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D860, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D860 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, for information purposes, I would like to put up on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we do this, by the way, sir, during your time in the Krajina, you were subjected to quite a bit of Serb propaganda against the Croat, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was constant, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was also beaten up, pistol-whipped, and robbed three times at gunpoint by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you not tell Mr. Stanton or during interview that when the events -- because of the period of time you this spent there and the time you had lived with the Serbs, that when Operation Storm took place, it was hard not to take the side of the Serbs. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't remember what I said, but I do remember that I lived with the Serbs and made friends with Serb. I never had a chance to do that on the Croatian side because I was never working in a Croatian area. So, yeah, I would agree that I knew the Serbs in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, when Operation Storm took place, you took the side of the Serbs, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: When Operation Storm was happening and I was beg shelled by the Croatian army, I didn't like it very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you said: "So, the answer to my question is yes ..." What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question, if we go back, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is what he said to Mr. Stanton, that was it was hard not to take the side of, isn't it? So you asked him what he said; and then to introduce that in the next question as, "So the answer to my question is yes, when Operation Storm took, place you took the side of the Serbs," that's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware of the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can split that up, Your Honour, and say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just inviting you not to suggest that the answer the witness gave is the answer as you formulated it, because that was not the answer he gave. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just clarify it by repeating the question, and that may be easier, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question was: "Did you not tell Mr. Stanton that because of the period of time you had spent there, meaning in the Krajina, and that time that you had lived with the Serbs, that when Operation Storm took place, it was hard not to take the side of the Serbs." Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I can't remember if I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you observe, during this period of time, that the Serbs that were working inside Sector South were attempting to influence the UN's perception of the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: If they were doing that, they did a very poor job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is 1D41-0149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we show the witness the statement, I would ask that we adhere to the procedure with regard to directing or questioning Mr. Dawes as to what he knows about a particular subject before he is shown what another witness says about a subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, until now only said that he is showing a statement. I have got no idea whether that is a statement of another witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adhere to the procedure that we first elicit from the witness the evidence he can give on it, and if there's then any reason to put the statement of another witness to the witness, you may do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for ease of reference, for the record, I will see whether or not he knows about this, but the statement I will be referring to, so Your Honour knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need, we'll find more about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this period, Mr. Dawes, did you know that the sole objective of the RSK was to obstruct the work of the UN -- excuse me, the ECMM and later the UN, that they did everything to keep the UN and ECMM from finding out the truth and repeatedly supplied them with misinformation? Were you aware that that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No. I would not be surprised if that was going on, but I wasn't directly aware that that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were aware, sir, that many of the UN personnel had become very close to the locals, had they not?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that includes Sergeant Engleby, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Sergeant Engleby with the Canadian Armed Forces, that is more than correct. He ended up marrying one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the contact with the local population became an area of concern for the UN, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to touch on a few matters concerning items that you talk about in your statement, and the first area that I'd like to address with you is that time just prior to Operation Storm. And you note in your 1996 statement at page 2, that, prior to the fall of Grahovo, morale was high. Then page 3 of your 1996 statement, you note that morale went through the basement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Toilet, basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there was a call-up of virtually all fighting personnel after the fall of Grahovo, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, tell us about the steps that were taken after the fall of Grahovo for the Serb population to leave the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Up to Grahovo, a couple of months before Grahovo fell, the RSK effectively sealed the border with Bosnia to stop its people from leaving. Obviously, they needed to have somebody there. When the possibility of Grahovo falling, which seemed absurd at one point, when Grahovo was sensed to be falling or there was a possibility that it could fail, the main supply route into Bosnia was opened and you could leave at your own leisure, I was told. I didn't see it with my own eyes. Sorry. Again, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, my question is: After the fall of Grahovo, tell us about the Serb population who left the area.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: It seemed like the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kehoe. That was not your question. The question was about steps that were taken after the fall of Grahovo for the Serb population to leave the Krajina. Of course, "steps taken" is not the same as people leaving the area, and I would like to have it cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will, Judge. I am trying. I will stay with this particular area, and I'm just letting the witness talk about that. But I will go with the question I had, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of course, I would be interested to know the answer to that question. So the witness then asked what the question was. Then let's put that question to him again, so we can hear his answer. What then later may have happened, whether people left, the question was about steps taken, were taken after the fall of Grahovo for the Serb population to leave the Krajina, and perhaps later we come to whether these steps were effective or not effective. So that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once Grahovo fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ignored Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I will let him answer the question. I just wanted to correct something on the transcript, and I will remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Please answer the question: What steps were taken after the fall of Grahovo for Serbs to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None that I could see, in the short answer, Your Honour. If anything, the population of Knin swelled to more people after the fall of Grahovo, and people were -- were waiting for the war to start. There was a general perception in town that -- that the Croatians were going to -- trying to retake back their land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were any efforts made for Serbs to leave?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: There was a severe fuel shortage in Knin, so I can't answer your question yes or no. I can just remember that a lot of people would have liked to have left, but there wasn't enough fuel for them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you try to get anybody out?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I tried to get one family out, tried. I offered my advice for them to get out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Gordana Zunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was Gordana Zunic?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Gordana Zunic was the translator for the accommodation section -- the camp services sections, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to get any other personnel out?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting in the pause, page 70, line -- the answer on line 11, I'm not sure that the witness answered the question in that way in the second sentence of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard him say something different as a matter of fact. When you were telling us about Sergeant Engleby, did he marry a local.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. On the transcript, it appears that you did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dawes, why did you want to get Gordana Zunic out?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: She was applying to become a Canadian citizen, and it would be a lot more difficult for her to continue her -- sorry, the paperwork, because she would have been dealing specifically with the Canadian embassy in Belgrade. Obviously, after Operation Storm, she would have to be dealing with the Croatian -- Canadian embassy in Zagreb. I don't even believe there was an official consulate then, or just a consulate, not a full-blown embassy. The paperwork started in Belgrade. It would be best for her to finish in Belgrade so she could become a Canadian citizen. That was started by previous French Canadian officers before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just looking at what you just said, I mean, Mr. Dawes, how did you know that prior to the morning of the 4th, that Ms. Zunic was going to end up in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I didn't. At least that's not what I meant to say. I didn't know she was going to end up in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 74, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't think I have page 74 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "I dont' even believe there was an official consulate then, or just a consulate, not a full-blown embassy. The paperwork started in Belgrade. It would be best for her to finish in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yeah, the paperwork for her Canadian citizen was started the year before in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the diary of Major Claude Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can to page for entry of the 29th, it would be page 31. If we can go three more pages up to 619, three more pages, please, and the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This talks about the -- well, at point 3: "The general mobilization is happening in town." Top of the next page: "Locals are leaving the area." And number 4, for the entry for the 30th -- excuse me, for the 29th: "Murray Dawes is trying to get Gordana, his interpreter/secretary, out." So we have a period of time from this where there is a general mobilisation. Major Bellerose says the locals are leaving, and at the same time, you're trying to get Gordona out. Is that time sequence correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to make an objection to the procedure being used here. I understand showing him the portion that says -- well, actually, I'm not sure I do understand. The witness -- the questions were asked of him about the general mobilisation. He was asked about locals leaving prior to Operation Storm, and he asked about whether or not he tried to help Gordana Zunic out. He gave answers to all of those. I would like to object to the witness being shown what is essentially the statement of another witness, whether to the effect that it agrees with what he said or disagrees with what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the guidance was that this evidence should be elicited first with the witness, which is has been done. Therefore, now if Mr. Kehoe wants to put further questions, of course if this would confirm, then, of course, then we would just establish that it corroborates. If it is something different, I think it should be clear from the question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, this is also an item which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this the sequence of events as to how the Gordana situation came up as laid out by Major --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... what exactly here is the sequence? Could you please illustrate for us what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The sequence of events is this, Judge: There is a general mobilization on the 28th. He notes that the locals are leaving. On the 29th, he notes that "Murray Dawes is trying to get Gordona out."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that your recollection as well, that that is how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the specific instance; but, in general, we were trying to get Gordana Zunic out to so she could become a Canadian citizen; not necessarily out of Knin, but, generally, out of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you were asked about this event, that is, you were trying to get Gordana Zunic out, in relation to other people leaving. That's, I think, the sequence we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, it is also the date. The date is of significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is why I'm talking about the sequence: What happened first, what next -- Mr. Russo, let's just see. In this diary, it's described that people are leaving the area, and that's described for the 28th. I can't see it on my screen anymore. And then on the 29th, it's described that you're trying to get Gordana out. Is that your recollection also as far as the sequence of events is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, at the run-up of storm, was there -- now, I'm just talking about just prior to Storm. Was there a movement, among the civilian population - I'm not about an organised movement - was there a movement just before Storm for the civilian population to leave the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: They were getting their ducks in a row in case that possibility happened. They were organising for that eventuality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How were they organising for that eventuality?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: What were the bus routes, were the buses still running, where can I buy petrol, issues like that, Where were we going to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn you to D514 in evidence, which is an article written by Major Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could if to the second page, the left hand column, towards the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes about halfway down that page: "Well, on the refugee side ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's toward the top now. Okay, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Well, on the refugee side, a lot of people from Knin fled that night just before the bombardment, just like someone had given them a heads autopsy and fled. It was apparently well organised." Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No. When you said the ramp-up to Desert Storm, you're talking about the few days before that, I am assuming?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you did not notice this incident that Major Bellerose is talking about the night before?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No. I'm sure you could ask him though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, just prior to Storm, you yourself had moved into -- or you had moved in UN Sector South, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Into the barracks, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date. A couple of months maybe, not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when we say "a couple of months," you are talking about you moved in sometime in June?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yeah. You know, I'm just throwing a dart at the dartboard. I wouldn't be able to tell you the specific date when he moved on to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, talking itself about the 4th of August, obviously, sir, you had no combat experience prior to the 4th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during the situation, I noticed during the course of your testimony that your tension and your fear factor naturally was quite high?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Off the scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, sir, you went out in this details to pick up personnel during the course of the morning of the 4th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as a result of this fear and tension, are you sure that your assessment not only the events but of the timing of your doing things are accurate?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: As best can be. I wasn't looking at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you notice -- I notice in your statement with regard to your first trip out -- and by the way, sir, you didn't feel like you were the proper person to go out and do this, did you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note that your first trip out - and I'm turning to the bottom of page 3, going over to page 4, to top - it was around 6.00. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Give or take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you say that -- just -- I don't want you to guess here because I just want you to look at your statement, and the actual time is set forth on page 4, approximately one, two, three -- seven lines from the top.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I guess my only point was that I might this statement 12 years ago; so, obviously, 12 years ago, I thought it was around 6.00 a.m. I don't know the exact time 12 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on that answer, you would say that what you wrote down 12 years ago was more reliable than what you can give us in 2008?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Obviously, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go through this statement, and you note in this that you pick up Alun Roberts first. He is the first person you pick up, and I believe that is on the top of page 4. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P276, page 16 -- excuse me, I'm sorry. P676, I apologise. 676, I misspoke, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the statement of Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be the third page in there. Two more pages, please, towards the bottom of that page: "At about 8.40 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that: "At around 8.40 hours that morning, Friday, 4 August, an UN armoured patrol carrier picked me up from outside my accommodation. Shells were still coming in, falling not only on the central government and military buildings of Knin but also on apartment blocks. One of the civilians picked up, and inside the armed patrol carrier was UN interpreter at Sector South, Gordana Zunic." If I may, just with -- and Mr. Dreyer, at 1789, talking about his third trip. 1789, line 2, where he certainly says that: "My third trip started 8.30, so I tuned [sic] just before 8.30." Bottom of that page line 55 at 1789: "Referring back to my statement, it indicates I departed at 8.30. "Q. And do you recall who went with you at that time? And you can refer back to your statement. "A. Reading my statement at paragraph 14, it indicates that I changed from a Jordanian APC to Czech APCs," and refers to, "I took Mr. Dawes with me." So that would be Murray Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No other Dawes. .

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be accurate to say that your first trip out was not at 6.00 but at 8.30, and that you went to pick up Gordana Zunic before you ever picked up Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No. I am saying that my story was that I left at that time in the morning, and either he is bad at timekeeping or I'm bad timekeeping. But on the first trip, it was our SOP to pick up Gordana Zunic because she was the person who had all the telephone numbers of everybody and where they lived in Knin. So that is why we picked her up on that trip. Now, whether we picked her up before Alun Roberts or after, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the timing of this trip, what time do you recall picking up Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Not a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to take a break at this time or you want to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If this is a suitable moment for you to have a break, then we'll have a break. We resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, I'd just like to talk to you about -- okay?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to talk to you about your first trip down to Knin on the 4thn, and it may be best to use P984.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I will be guided by what Your Honour thinks. Frankly, I have to agree with my learned friend that the digitally-enhanced photograph is better than that which will come up as 984 which is on the screen. We may want to put up just to see how it looks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the hard copy at least of the digitally-enhanced copy with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it has been uploaded as 5961, so we can pull it up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could do that, that would be helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. 5961 appears to be the same as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's work on the basis of this document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that will work, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the one I prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, just taking your testimony and the drawings that you made, the first place you stopped going around the road was D, the bus station, and A, the ARSK headquarters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Definitely D, the bus station, and I think there's an interpretation of what the headquarters building is. Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just reading your P981, paragraph 9, maybe you can help us on that.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Okay. That's correct. The bus station and the parliament building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And F would be the radio station. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Yeah, Radio Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted in your statement, your 1996 statement, at page 4, that when you got to this location, the shelling was quite intense.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not sure if this D marking is correct. Paragraph 8 indicates that the bus station was marked as D, but the following paragraph indicates that the parliament building next door to the HQ and the location of both is marked as A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I thought that what's he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think what came out of the transcript, is that the parliament as at D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's what is stated. I think the witness said "A." With all due respect, Mr. Dawes, I do believe that Mr. Dawes said that the bus station was D and that the headquarter area was A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that's what you put to him and that's what he confirmed, although not very clear, in relation to A. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were there, Mr. Dawes, did it strike you or did you concluded that the HV was trying to knock out the command and control and the communication compatibilities of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't believe I thought of it that way. I just thought that -- it's the first time I have ever been shelled before, so I just realized that the shelling was extremely heavy, and they were targeting both sides of the road: The railway yard and the -- the bus station side and the Radio Knin side of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it was during this period of time where you noted for us that you saw some ARSK soldiers in the area, pointed B?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that, in your statement in 2008, paragraph 10, that these young soldiers were not part of any unit or operation in the area, and that there was six of them. Where did these soldiers come from?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: They were on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where were they before they were on the street?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I have no idea. When we -- as I recollected, as we turned the corner up the hill, they were on the road by the time we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know if they were part of any unit?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if you don't know that, you wouldn't know if they were assigned to some type of military operation that morning, do you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you discuss with these soldiers anything about where the rest of their unit - assuming they had one - the rest of their unit was?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it strike you at that time, sir, that the shelling that was going on was causing the ARSK military, at least these soldiers, to panic?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I would say that their general state of behaviour was very close to panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it, likewise, strike you that as a result of this panic, these soldiers warranted to get out of the area?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted during the course of your direct testimony and your statement, when you were in the location around F and B, you observed civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Between F and B, in that general area, so on the side -- they were on sides of roads, like the sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would that be in the area that was near to the parliament, the Radio Knin, and the ARSK headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: As well as residential buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you've noted for us previously that it was very difficult to tell whether or not somebody was a civilian or whether or not that person was military?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object that. I don't think the witness ever said it was difficult to make that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, the witness explained what he had to take into account when assessing whether someone would have been a military or a civilian person, and we did not hear the person that he was ever in a position to verify finally whether the first impression the was correct one, yes or no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, you would agree with me that the males that you saw dead on the street, you don't know if they were military or civilian, do you?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Categorically, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you talked a little bit about riding through this area in your 1996 statement and talked about going into the Tvik factory. Now, the Tvik was a screw factory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they supplying anything that they made in the Tvik factory to the ARSK military; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I never saw anything been manufactured there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Answer my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know if they were supplying the ARSK military with anything that they made there?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I don't know if they're supplying anything to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also noted during, the course of your direct examination, that the railroad was being shelled but was not in use. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you P804, an ECMM report of 4 August 1995. Paragraph 4: "On economical and industrial and infrastructural, obviously a lot of damage during the day. Trains are seen being moved in Knin. Comment: Presumably used for military purpose, but these could be used for evacuation of civilians. End comment." I take it that you didn't observe that movement of trains that ECMM saw?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you discuss it with anybody that trains had been moving in the yards on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the situation with regard to the school. And by the way, sir, the school that you testified from the photograph -- I don't know the number of the photograph off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. P982.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You heard from somebody else that had been destroyed, I think you -- totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do know that in the 4th of August, 1995, no schools were in session.

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know, or do you know now, or did you know then what arms of the RSK government were housed at that facility?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apology, Your Honour. I'll pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This would be - excuse me - D718, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dawes, on the item marked G, were you aware that there was a school there and that Serb soldiers were garrisoned in that location on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: No, I would not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to P78. This is a map drawn by Mr. Dreyer. If I could have the left-hand side which is around the letter C, and if I could just blow that up. On the left-hand side, just to see it. Okay. I know it's a little difficult to see it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that location, C, Mr. Dawes?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: I do -- sorry. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dreyer informed this Court that that was a school that had a mortar emplacement or the morning of the 4th, and that would be Mr. Dreyer's testimony at ... [Overlapping speakers] ... 1721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that putting the statements of Mr. Dreyer to the witness -- he hasn't asked the witness whether or not he saw anything at that particular school --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll ask it again, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought he was talking about a different school. If he was referring to this one, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regards to C?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: With regard to C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know there is a school where C is?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES
utterances.text: Just so we're speaking clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
